question: What is Java Flight Recorder (JFR)?
options: A build plugin that formats Java source files
A low-overhead event recording framework built into the JVM for diagnostics and profiling
A catalog service for third-party Java libraries
A tool that executes Java methods on remote servers
explanation: JFR is a built-in JVM facility that records runtime events (CPU samples, GC, locks, I/O, JIT and so on) with low overhead so they can be analyzed later. It is not a build or deployment tool.

question: In which Java release was JFR open-sourced in OpenJDK through JEP 328?
explanation: JEP 328 contributed JFR to OpenJDK in Java 11. Earlier it was a commercial feature of Oracle JDK 7/8. Because of this, any Java 17 runtime includes JFR with no license unlock.

question: Assume Java 17 on Linux. Which command starts the application with a recording that runs for 60 seconds and is saved to rec.jfr?
explanation: Recordings are started at launch with -XX:StartFlightRecording and comma-separated parameters such as duration and filename. The other flags do not exist; no commercial unlock is needed in modern JDKs.

question: A production JVM with process id 4242 is already running without any recording. Which command starts a JFR recording without restarting it?
explanation: jcmd sends diagnostic commands to a running JVM, and JFR.start begins a recording dynamically. jstat and jmap have no JFR switch and javac is only the compiler.

question: What is the practical difference between the default and profile settings when starting a JFR recording?
options: profile disables all garbage collection events
profile is identical to default but writes to another file
profile enables more detailed events and higher sampling rates, at somewhat higher overhead than default
explanation: The profile configuration is intended for short investigations: it samples more often and enables more events. The default configuration is tuned for very low overhead so it can run continuously.

question: A recording named r1 is running in JVM 4242. Which command writes the data collected so far to disk without ending the recording?
explanation: JFR.dump copies the current contents of a running recording to a file while it continues to run. JFR.save, JFR.write and JFR.export are not JFR diagnostic commands.

question: Which JDK command-line tool prints the events stored in a .jfr file in readable form (Java 17)?
explanation: The jfr tool shipped with the JDK has subcommands such as print, summary, assemble and disassemble. javap disassembles class files, jstack prints thread stacks and jdeps analyzes dependencies.

question: Which jfr subcommand prints how many events of each type a recording file contains (Java 17)?
explanation: jfr summary reports metadata and per-event-type counts and sizes, which is a quick way to see what a recording contains before looking at details with jfr print.

question: Assume Java 17. A teammate who read newer documentation runs: jfr view hot-methods rec.jfr. What is the most likely result?
options: The command fails because the view subcommand does not exist in this release; it was introduced in a later one
explanation: The jfr view subcommand was added in Java 21. In Java 17 use jfr print (optionally with --events) or open the file in JDK Mission Control. This is a typical version-dependent trap.

question: Why is JFR considered suitable for use in production?
options: It pauses all application threads during every sample
It dumps the whole heap for each event
It only works in debug builds of the JVM
Events are written to thread-local buffers by the JVM itself, and the default configuration targets very low overhead
explanation: JFR is built into the JVM and records events into buffers with minimal synchronization. The default settings aim for roughly 1% overhead or less. Overhead still depends on which events and thresholds you enable.

question: Assume Java 17 and that no JFR recording is running. What is the output?
options: An exception is thrown because no recording is active
A compile error because Event cannot be subclassed
explanation: Custom events are ordinary classes extending jdk.jfr.Event. When no recording has the event enabled, begin() and commit() are cheap no-ops, so the program simply continues and prints done.

question: Which method completes the code so that the fields are filled and committed only when the event is enabled and its duration meets the configured threshold?
explanation: shouldCommit() returns true only if the event is enabled and its duration reaches the threshold, which avoids computing expensive field values for events that would be dropped. isEnabled() ignores the threshold, and the other two methods do not exist.

question: What happens when this code is compiled?
options: It runs and prints ok, but the event is ignored at runtime
It compiles with a warning only
It fails to compile because TaskEvent does not extend jdk.jfr.Event, so begin() and commit() are not defined
explanation: begin() and commit() are inherited from jdk.jfr.Event. Without extending it, the compiler reports a cannot-find-symbol error. This is a compile-time error, not a runtime one.

question: Which statement best summarizes how JFR stores recorded events?
options: Events go into thread-local buffers, are flushed to global buffers, and are then written to chunk files on disk or kept in memory
Every event is sent over the network to JDK Mission Control immediately
Events are kept only as Java objects on the application heap
Events are written to standard output and must be redirected
explanation: JFR avoids contention by writing into thread-local buffers first, then flushing to global buffers and to chunks in a repository. A recording can later be dumped to a .jfr file.

question: How does async-profiler collect Java stack traces with low overhead and without requiring safepoints?
options: By walking the heap with JVMTI only
By instrumenting the bytecode of every method
By using AsyncGetCallTrace together with OS-level sampling such as perf_events or timers
By running jstack once per second
explanation: async-profiler triggers samples through the OS (perf_events, timer signals) and obtains Java stacks through AsyncGetCallTrace, so threads need not reach a safepoint and no bytecode instrumentation is used.

question: A service has a high p99 latency but low CPU usage because threads mostly wait on a database and locks. Which async-profiler event mode best shows where threads spend their elapsed time?
explanation: Wall-clock mode samples threads regardless of whether they run, sleep or block, so waiting time becomes visible. cpu and itimer only capture on-CPU time and alloc shows allocation sites.

question: Assume Linux and async-profiler installed at /opt/ap. Which command starts the JVM with async-profiler and writes a CPU flame graph to flame.html?
explanation: async-profiler is a native agent, so it is loaded with -agentpath (not -javaagent, which expects a jar). The argument string selects start, the event type and the output file; the .html extension selects flame graph output.

question: How should the horizontal axis of a flame graph be read?
options: Chronological time from left to right
The id of the sampled thread
Frames are merged and sorted by name, and a frame's width is proportional to the number of samples containing it
explanation: A flame graph is not a timeline. Identical stack prefixes are merged, so width shows how often a frame appeared in samples. Left-to-right order has no time meaning.

question: In a CPU flame graph, which area usually points to the best optimization candidates?
options: Wide frames at the top (leaf) edge, where the time is actually spent
The bottom frame such as main
explanation: Wide plateaus at the top show code that is itself consuming many samples. Tall narrow towers only mean deep call stacks, and bottom frames are wide for almost every program because all samples pass through them.

question: Assume / means integer division. What is printed?
explanation: A appears 5 times, so count is 5 and 5 * 100 / 8 = 500 / 8 = 62 with integer division. The exact share is 62.5%, but the convention truncates it.

question: A sampling profiler takes one sample every 20 ms and a method appears in 150 samples. What does the pseudocode print as the estimated time in milliseconds?
code:
interval_ms = 20
total = 0
for i in 1..150:
    total = total + interval_ms
print(total)
explanation: The loop adds 20 exactly 150 times, so total is 3000. Sampling estimates time as sample count multiplied by the interval, which is statistical and not an exact measurement.

question: Convention: s contains ";a;" is true when the substring occurs in s. What is printed?
explanation: Three of the four merged stacks pass through frame a, so its flame graph width is 3 out of 4 samples, which is 75 percent. The stack main;d does not contain a.

question: Assume Java 17. Which startup option keeps a rolling window of roughly the last 30 minutes of events on disk so that it can be dumped after an incident?
explanation: A recording with disk=true and maxage=30m continuously discards older data and can be dumped with JFR.dump on demand. duration=30m stops the recording after 30 minutes, delay only postpones the start, and FlightRecorderOptions configures the repository but starts no recording.

question: Which statement about stack frames is correct when comparing JFR and async-profiler?
options: Only JFR can show native and kernel frames
async-profiler can include native and kernel frames in its stacks, while JFR focuses on Java frames
Neither tool can show anything except Java frames
Both always show identical native frames
explanation: Because async-profiler samples through the OS, it can attach native and kernel frames to Java stacks, which helps find time spent in libc, the JVM itself or system calls. JFR execution samples are primarily Java stacks.

question: What is the purpose of the JVM flag -XX:+DebugNonSafepoints when profiling?
options: It disables safepoints in the JVM
It records debug information at non-safepoint locations so samples can be attributed to precise lines and inlined methods
It enables a debug build of the JIT compiler
It writes a core dump when the JVM crashes
explanation: Without this flag the JIT only emits metadata at safepoint locations, so samples taken elsewhere can be attributed to nearby, less accurate frames. The flag needs -XX:+UnlockDiagnosticVMOptions and improves attribution accuracy.

question: On Linux, async-profiler cannot use perf_events for a non-root user. Which command relaxes the kernel setting as recommended for user-space profiling?
explanation: kernel.perf_event_paranoid controls who may use perf events. Lowering it (and setting kernel.kptr_restrict=0 for kernel symbols) lets async-profiler use perf_events. The other settings are unrelated.

question: Which JFR event, available in Java 17, provides sampled information about object allocations?
explanation: jdk.ObjectAllocationSample (introduced in Java 16) is a throttled allocation event that records weighted samples with stack traces. The other names are not real JFR events.

question: Which JFR event helps find memory leak candidates by sampling long-lived objects?
explanation: jdk.OldObjectSample tracks a sample of objects that stay alive for a long time and can include the reference chain to GC roots, which points toward what keeps them reachable.

question: What does the path-to-gc-roots=true parameter do in commands like jcmd 4242 JFR.dump path-to-gc-roots=true filename=/tmp/leak.jfr?
options: Dumps the whole heap in HPROF format
Triggers a full garbage collection and stops the JVM
Lists the classpath entries of the application
Records the reference chain from sampled old objects to GC roots, which costs extra time at dump time
explanation: The reference chain tells you why an object is still reachable, which is what you need to fix a leak. Computing it is expensive, so it is done when the recording is dumped rather than continuously.

question: Which method completes the code to count GC events in a recording file?
explanation: RecordingFile exposes hasMoreEvents() and readEvent(), which throws an IOException at the end of data. The other names do not exist in the jdk.jfr.consumer API.

question: Which Java class (available since Java 14) lets an application consume JFR events in-process while they are being produced?
explanation: RecordingStream, introduced by JEP 349 (event streaming), lets you register handlers per event type and receive events continuously. RecordingFile only reads a finished file.

question: A service has a p99 latency of 2 seconds, but the async-profiler cpu flame graph shows only small, scattered hotspots. What is the most likely reason?
options: The flame graph hides hot methods by design
cpu mode samples only on-CPU time, so threads blocked on I/O or locks do not appear
cpu mode profiles only the garbage collector
Flame graphs cannot be used for latency
explanation: If threads are waiting rather than running, a CPU profile has no samples for that time. Use wall-clock or lock profiling (or JFR I/O and monitor events) to see blocking time.

question: Many threads wait on synchronized blocks and ReentrantLock objects. Which async-profiler event shows where time is lost waiting for locks?
explanation: The lock event profiles contention on Java monitors and java.util.concurrent locks and attributes the waiting time to the stack that waited. alloc, cpu and itimer measure other resources.

question: Which JFR event records threads blocked while trying to enter a synchronized block?
explanation: jdk.JavaMonitorEnter is emitted when a thread has to wait to acquire a monitor and its duration exceeds the threshold. It is the JFR counterpart of monitor contention profiling.

question: Which rule best summarizes a sound profiling workflow?
options: Use a representative workload, find the real hotspot with a profiler, change one thing, and measure again
Guess the slowest method, rewrite it, and ship without measuring
Enable every event at maximum detail on all production JVMs permanently
Profile only an idle application on a laptop
explanation: Profiling results are only meaningful under realistic load, and every change must be verified by measurement. Changing many things at once or guessing makes it impossible to know what helped.

question: Which JFR event records the duration of an individual phase of a stop-the-world garbage collection pause?
explanation: jdk.GCPhasePause (with its Level variants) records pause phases of the collector. This is what you inspect when GC pauses contribute to latency.

question: With the default settings, jdk.FileRead events do not appear for file reads that take 1 ms. Why?
options: JFR cannot observe file I/O at all
FileRead is recorded only during heap dumps
Duration-based events have a configurable threshold, and faster operations are not recorded
explanation: To limit overhead, I/O and lock events are written only when their duration reaches a threshold (20 ms by default for file I/O). Lowering the threshold in the settings records more events but increases overhead and file size.

question: Which async-profiler agent argument produces a JFR-format file that JDK Mission Control can open?
explanation: async-profiler selects the output format from the file extension: .jfr gives JFR format, .html gives a flame graph, .collapsed gives collapsed stacks and .txt gives a text report.

question: When is JFR a better choice than async-profiler?
options: When you need kernel and native frames in the same stack
When you must profile a non-HotSpot VM
When you want a JDK-built-in recorder that combines CPU samples, GC, JIT, I/O and lock events in one file without installing a native agent
When you need hardware cache-miss counters
explanation: JFR ships with the JDK and records a wide set of JVM events together, which is ideal where installing native tools is restricted. async-profiler is stronger for native/kernel frames and perf counters.

question: Which jfr print option limits the output to named event types (Java 17)?
explanation: jfr print supports --events followed by a comma-separated list of event names, which avoids dumping a very large recording in full. The other switches do not exist.

question: A wall-clock profile of a service is dominated by frames such as Unsafe.park inside worker threads. What is the most appropriate interpretation?
options: Idle pool threads waiting for work are sampled too, so you should focus on request-handling stacks or filter threads
The JIT inlined every park call
explanation: Wall-clock mode samples all threads whether running or waiting, so idle workers appear as wide parked frames. They are not a bottleneck; look at the frames of threads that actually handle requests.

question: A teammate says: "JFR is always under 1% overhead, so I will enable all events with threshold 0 in production." What is correct?
options: Correct, overhead is fixed regardless of settings
Correct, JFR automatically disables expensive events
Incorrect, only heap dumps are expensive
Incorrect, the low overhead applies to the default settings; very frequent events with zero thresholds can add significant cost and data volume
explanation: The overhead figure refers to the curated default configuration. Enabling high-frequency events such as I/O or monitor events with no threshold can produce huge amounts of data and slow the application.

question: What is printed? (Assume Java 17.)
options: true, then false on the next line
true, then true on the next line
false, then false on the next line
false, then true on the next line
explanation: Both loops build the text 01234, so equals returns true. toString() creates a new String object, so reference comparison with == is false. The first loop also allocates several intermediate Strings, which is exactly what an allocation profile would reveal.

question: Which code correctly records only GC events programmatically with the JFR API and writes them to x.jfr (Java 17; work() is defined elsewhere)?
options: try (Recording r = new Recording()) { r.enable("jdk.GarbageCollection"); r.start(); work(); r.stop(); r.dump(Path.of("x.jfr")); }
explanation: jdk.jfr.Recording is the API class: enable the desired event, start, stop and then dump to a Path. Recording implements AutoCloseable. The other calls are not part of the API.

question: Which statement about async-profiler's alloc event is correct?
options: It identifies the objects that are retained and leaking
It works only with the G1 collector
It shows where allocations happen (sampled), not which objects stay alive; use heap analysis or old-object sampling for leaks
explanation: Allocation profiling reports allocation sites weighted by size, which helps reduce allocation rate. A site that allocates a lot is not necessarily leaking, because the objects may be short-lived.

question: Which statement about attaching async-profiler to a running JVM is correct?
options: The profiler must run as the same user as the target JVM, or with suitable privileges
The JVM must have been started with -javaagent
The JVM must have been started with -Xdebug
JFR must be running at the same time
explanation: Dynamic attach uses the JVM attach mechanism, which normally requires the same user and a reachable process. No special startup flag is required for basic profiling, though extra flags such as DebugNonSafepoints improve accuracy.

question: A custom JFR event is enabled. A developer calls begin(), performs work, and then calls commit() without calling end(). What happens?
options: commit() ends the event automatically, so the duration covers the time since begin()
explanation: If end() has not been called, commit() sets the end time itself, so the event records a duration from begin() to commit(). Calling end() explicitly is only needed when you want to stop timing earlier.

question: Convention: an event is recorded when its duration is greater than or equal to the threshold. What is printed?
code:
durations_ms = [5, 25, 30, 10, 20, 40]
threshold_ms = 20
recorded = 0
for d in durations_ms:
    if d >= threshold_ms:
        recorded = recorded + 1
print(recorded)
explanation: The values 25, 30, 20 and 40 are at or above 20, so four events are recorded. The value 20 counts because the comparison is inclusive.

question: A flame graph shows 40% of CPU samples under JSON serialization frames. What is the best next step?
options: Rewrite the serializer in assembly immediately
Examine the call paths leading into serialization, find avoidable work such as repeated serialization, and confirm any improvement with a measurement
explanation: The flame graph tells you where time goes, not why. Inspecting callers reveals whether work is redundant. After a change, re-profile or benchmark to prove the gain.

question: Which JFR event samples threads that are currently executing native code?
explanation: jdk.ExecutionSample covers threads running Java code, while jdk.NativeMethodSample covers threads in native methods. A thread blocked in a native call is therefore missing from the first event type.

question: Which tool is the standard graphical application for opening and analyzing JFR recordings?
explanation: JDK Mission Control (JMC) opens .jfr files and offers views and automated analysis. It is distributed separately from the JDK since Java 11.

question: Which strategy is recommended for using JFR in a production service?
options: Always use the profile configuration with every threshold set to 0
Keep a low-overhead continuous recording with default settings, and start a short, more detailed recording only while investigating
Run profilers only inside unit tests
explanation: A continuous default recording gives history for post-mortem analysis at low cost. Detailed settings add overhead, so they should be limited in time and scope.

question: perf_events are unavailable in a restricted container. Which async-profiler event is a CPU-sampling fallback that does not need them?
explanation: itimer mode uses the ITIMER_PROF timer signal, so it works where perf_events are blocked, with somewhat less precision. alloc and lock sample other resources and wall measures elapsed time, not CPU.

question: Why should CPU profiles of a Java service usually be taken after a warm-up period?
options: Early samples include interpreter execution and JIT compilation activity that is not representative of steady-state performance
JFR cannot record during the first minute
Garbage collection does not run before warm-up
explanation: At startup the JVM interprets code and compiles hot methods, so the profile shows different behavior from the optimized steady state. Profile under realistic load once the code is warm unless startup itself is the target.

question: Which JFR event helps analyze time spent in JIT compilation?
explanation: jdk.Compilation records JIT compilations with their duration and method, which helps explain warm-up delays or CPU spent in compiler threads.

question: What is printed?
explanation: The loop keeps the name with the highest sample count. Because 30 is the unique maximum, best ends as worker-2 regardless of iteration order, and the program prints the name, not the count.

question: Which diagnostic command lists the active recordings of JVM 4242 together with their ids and names?
explanation: JFR.check shows the state of all recordings in the target JVM. The other command names are not valid JFR diagnostic commands.

question: Why can instrumenting every method with bytecode distort a profile compared with sampling?
options: It makes the JVM skip garbage collection
It adds per-call overhead and changes JIT inlining, so tiny hot methods can look much costlier than they are
It works only for static methods
explanation: Instrumentation adds code to every call, which perturbs what the JIT can inline and optimize. Sampling observes the running program periodically, so its overhead does not scale with call counts.

question: Which command stops recording r1 in JVM 4242 and writes it to /tmp/out.jfr?
explanation: JFR.stop ends a named recording and, when filename is given, writes its data to that file. The other command names and parameter names are invalid.

question: Which statement correctly describes safepoint bias in sampling profilers?
options: Samples are distributed evenly, so no bias exists
The profiler prefers sampling threads with the highest priority
Samples are taken only at safepoint polls, so time in code without polls, such as some counted loops, is under-reported or attributed to nearby safepoints
The bias occurs only when the garbage collector is running
explanation: Profilers that stop threads at safepoints can only observe code locations where a poll exists, which misrepresents where time is spent. JFR and async-profiler avoid this by sampling asynchronously.

question: What is a heap dump?
options: A list of all threads and their stack traces
A log of all garbage collection pauses
A snapshot of the objects in the Java heap at a point in time, including their fields and references
A copy of the JIT-compiled native code cache
explanation: A heap dump (usually an HPROF file) captures the live object graph: instances, their field values, arrays and class information. Thread stacks are shown by a thread dump, and GC pauses are recorded in GC logs or JFR.

question: Which command writes a heap dump of the running JVM with process id 4242 to /tmp/heap.hprof (Java 17)?
explanation: GC.heap_dump is the jcmd diagnostic command that writes an HPROF heap dump. Thread.print prints stack traces, and the other command names are not valid.

question: Which JDK tool prints the stack traces of all threads of the JVM with process id 4242?
explanation: jstack attaches to a running JVM and prints a thread dump. jstat reports GC statistics, jmap works with heap information, and javap disassembles class files.

question: On Linux, which command makes a running JVM with process id 4242 print a thread dump to its standard output without terminating it?
explanation: Signal 3 (SIGQUIT) tells HotSpot to print a thread dump to the process's stdout and continue running. Signals 9, 15 and 2 terminate the process.

question: In a thread dump, which Thread.State does a thread have while it waits to enter a synchronized block whose monitor is held by another thread?
explanation: BLOCKED means the thread is trying to acquire a monitor lock held by another thread. WAITING and TIMED_WAITING apply to Object.wait, join, park and sleep, not to monitor entry.

question: Assume Java 17. Which command line makes the JVM write a heap dump into the directory /dumps when it throws an OutOfMemoryError for the Java heap?
explanation: HeapDumpOnOutOfMemoryError enables the automatic dump and HeapDumpPath selects the file or directory. The other flags are not HotSpot options.

question: Assume Java 17. What is printed on the two lines?
explanation: Before start() a thread is NEW. After join() returns, the thread has finished its run method, so its state is TERMINATED.

question: What is printed? (Assume normal scheduling.)
explanation: Thread.sleep with a timeout puts the thread into TIMED_WAITING. After 300 ms the worker is still inside its 2000 ms sleep.

question: What is printed? (Assume normal scheduling.)
explanation: Object.wait() without a timeout moves the thread to WAITING and releases the monitor. It is not BLOCKED, because it is not competing for a monitor at that moment.

question: What is printed? (Assume normal scheduling.)
explanation: The main thread holds the monitor while the worker tries to enter the synchronized block, so the worker is BLOCKED until main leaves the block.

question: What does a stack line such as "- waiting to lock <0x000000076ab62208>" in a thread dump mean?
options: The thread owns the monitor at that address
The thread is trying to acquire the monitor at that address, which another thread currently holds
The thread called Object.wait() on that monitor
The thread is sleeping while holding that monitor
explanation: "waiting to lock" marks a thread that is BLOCKED on a monitor. Search the dump for "locked <same address>" to find the owner. A thread inside Object.wait() is shown with "waiting on" instead.

question: Assume typical scheduling. What happens when this program runs?
options: It prints t1, then t2, then done
It throws IllegalMonitorStateException from one thread
Neither t1, t2 nor done is printed, because both threads wait forever and the program never terminates
explanation: Each thread takes its first lock, sleeps, and then asks for the lock the other thread holds. This is a classic lock-ordering deadlock. A thread dump of this process would report a Java-level deadlock between Thread-0 and Thread-1.

question: Which part of a jstack output tells you that the JVM detected a monitor deadlock?
options: A heap summary section listing generation sizes
A section starting with "Found one Java-level deadlock" that lists the threads and the locks they wait for
explanation: jstack and jcmd Thread.print run the JVM's deadlock detector and append a deadlock section naming the threads involved and which lock each holds and wants.

question: Two threads deadlock because one locks A then B while the other locks B then A. Which fix removes the deadlock?
options: Raise the priority of one thread
Call Thread.yield() before taking the second lock
Acquire the locks in the same global order in every thread
explanation: A consistent lock ordering removes the circular wait that deadlock needs. Priorities, yield and volatile do not change the fact that each thread holds one lock while waiting for another.

question: Why is it recommended to take several thread dumps a few seconds apart instead of only one?
options: To see which threads stay at the same place across dumps, separating stuck threads from transient activity
Because a JVM can include only one thread per dump
Because the first dump is always discarded
explanation: A thread dump is a single snapshot. A thread that shows the same stack in several dumps is likely stuck or looping, while one that appears once may be doing normal short work.

question: On Linux, top -H shows a hot thread with id 12345. The command below converts it for matching nid=0x... in a jstack dump. What does it print?
code: printf '%x\n' 12345
explanation: 12345 in decimal is 0x3039 (3*4096 + 0*256 + 3*16 + 9). printf with %x prints the hex digits without a 0x prefix. In the dump you search for nid=0x3039.

question: Retained size is the memory that would be freed if an object were garbage collected. Assume objects are reachable only along the listed references. What is printed?
code:
sizes: A=16, B=24, C=40, D=16
references: root -> A, root -> D, A -> B, A -> C, D -> C
retained = 0
for X in [A, B, C, D]:
    if X is unreachable from root after removing the edge root -> A:
        retained = retained + size(X)
print(retained)
explanation: Without the edge to A, objects A and B become unreachable (16 + 24 = 40). C stays reachable through D, so it is not part of A's retained size.

question: Which statement correctly distinguishes shallow size and retained size in heap analysis?
options: Shallow size includes all objects referenced by the object, while retained size does not
Retained size counts only primitive fields
Shallow size is the memory used by the object itself; retained size is the memory that would be freed if the object were collected
explanation: Shallow size covers only the object's own header and fields. Retained size also includes everything kept alive exclusively through that object, which makes it the better metric for finding leaks.

question: Which tool is widely used to open and analyze .hprof heap dump files?
explanation: Eclipse MAT parses HPROF dumps and provides histograms, a dominator tree and leak reports. javap, jlink and jshell have nothing to do with heap analysis.

question: In heap analysis, what does it mean that object X dominates object Y?
options: Every path from a GC root to Y passes through X, so Y is retained only by X
X holds a weak reference to Y
explanation: Dominance is defined on paths from GC roots. If X dominates Y, collecting X would also make Y unreachable. The dominator tree built from this relation is the basis of retained-size calculations.

question: Which of the following is a GC root?
options: An object referenced only by another unreachable object
A local variable reference on the stack of a live thread
An object whose class overrides finalize()
An object that has not been accessed for a long time
explanation: GC roots include local variables and parameters on live thread stacks, static fields, active threads and JNI references. Reachability from a root, not age or access time, decides whether an object is kept.

question: What does java.lang.OutOfMemoryError: Metaspace usually indicate?
options: The young generation is too small
The application created too many threads
Too much class metadata is loaded, often because of class or classloader leaks
explanation: Metaspace holds class metadata in native memory. Exhausting it typically points to classes that cannot be unloaded, for example after repeated redeploys, or to heavy runtime class generation.

question: What does java.lang.OutOfMemoryError: GC overhead limit exceeded mean?
options: The heap dump file exceeded its size limit
One pause missed its target time
The JVM is spending an excessive share of time in garbage collection while reclaiming very little memory
explanation: The parallel collectors throw this error when almost all time goes to GC and almost nothing is freed. It usually means the live set nearly fills the heap, so a heap dump is the right next step.

question: Assume Java 17. A developer wants a heap dump that also contains unreachable objects that have not yet been collected. Which command does that?
options: jcmd 4242 GC.heap_dump /tmp/h.hprof, because the default includes unreachable objects
explanation: By default jcmd GC.heap_dump dumps only reachable objects (it triggers a full GC first). The -all option includes unreachable objects as well. The trap is assuming the default is the larger, unfiltered dump.

question: What does the live option do in jmap -dump:live,format=b,file=h.hprof 4242?
options: It lets the JVM keep running, while without it the JVM exits
It dumps only reachable objects and forces a full GC first
explanation: With live, jmap triggers a full collection and writes only objects that survive. Without live, all objects, including garbage not yet collected, are written. The full GC means a visible pause.

question: Which method completes the code so that it writes a heap dump of only live objects?
explanation: HotSpotDiagnosticMXBean.dumpHeap(String outputFile, boolean live) writes an HPROF file. The file name must end with .hprof, and live=true restricts the dump to reachable objects.

question: Which command prints an instance count and byte total per class without writing a full heap dump file (Java 17)?
explanation: GC.class_histogram prints a per-class histogram of instances and sizes. GC.heap_info only summarizes heap regions, VM.flags lists JVM flags, and Thread.print prints stacks.

question: In a class histogram, what type does the entry [B represent?
explanation: Array classes use JVM descriptors: [B is byte[], [C is char[], [I is int[] and [Z is boolean[]. Since Java 9 compact strings, byte[] is usually large because Strings store their content in it.

question: Two class histograms (instance counts) were taken one hour apart. What is printed?
explanation: Growth is 500 for String, 100 for byte[] and 4000 for Order. Comparing snapshots over time and looking at the class that grows fastest is a standard first step when hunting a leak.

question: Which expression completes the code so that the cache keeps at most three entries and the program prints [3, 4, 5]?
explanation: removeEldestEntry is called after each insertion. Returning true only when the size exceeds MAX evicts the least recently used entry and keeps the map bounded, which prevents the unbounded cache growth that often shows up as a leak in heap dumps.

question: A long-running service stores one entry per request id in a static HashMap and never removes entries. What will heap dumps taken hours apart show?
options: A shrinking number of HashMap nodes
Constant counts for all application classes
Growing numbers of map nodes and values, all retained through the static map, which has a very large retained size
explanation: Static fields are GC roots, so everything reachable from that map stays alive. In the dominator tree the map appears as a top consumer, and its growth between dumps identifies the leak.

question: Request handlers run on pooled threads and store a large object in a ThreadLocal named TL. Which implementation avoids retaining the object after the request ends?
options: TL.set(big); handle(); // pooled threads clear their ThreadLocals when a task ends
try { TL.set(big); handle(); } catch (Exception e) { TL.remove(); }
explanation: Pool threads live for a long time, so values stored in their ThreadLocal maps stay reachable until removed. Removing in finally covers both normal and exceptional exits. Removing only on exceptions or before set leaves the value in place on the normal path.

question: A container's resident memory keeps growing, but heap dumps and GC logs show a stable heap. What is the most likely explanation and next tool?
options: The growth is in native memory outside the heap, such as direct buffers, thread stacks or metaspace; enable Native Memory Tracking and inspect it with jcmd VM.native_memory
The heap dump was taken from the wrong JVM, so only heap tuning can help
Garbage collection is disabled once resident memory exceeds -Xmx
Only young generation objects are growing, and they never appear in a heap dump
explanation: A heap dump only covers Java objects on the heap. Direct ByteBuffers, thread stacks, metaspace, code cache and native libraries use other memory. -XX:NativeMemoryTracking=summary together with jcmd VM.native_memory breaks it down by category.

question: A container is terminated by the Linux OOM killer (exit code 137) although the JVM was started with -XX:+HeapDumpOnOutOfMemoryError. Is a heap dump expected?
options: Yes, the JVM catches SIGKILL and writes the dump before exiting
Yes, but only when the G1 collector is used
No, SIGKILL ends the process immediately and no OutOfMemoryError was thrown, so the flag never takes effect
No, because heap dumps are only supported on Windows
explanation: The flag works only when the JVM itself throws OutOfMemoryError. A kill by the kernel or cgroup limit cannot be intercepted, so no dump is produced. Use container-aware heap sizing and native memory tracking to investigate.

question: Which event does NOT trigger a dump when the JVM runs with -XX:+HeapDumpOnOutOfMemoryError?
options: A StackOverflowError caused by unbounded recursion
explanation: The flag reacts to OutOfMemoryError conditions raised by the JVM. A StackOverflowError is a different error about thread stack depth, so it produces no heap dump.

question: Assume Windows and a Java application running in a console window. Which key combination makes the JVM print a thread dump to that console?
explanation: On Windows, Ctrl+Break delivers the equivalent of SIGQUIT and prints a thread dump. Ctrl+C sends an interrupt that normally terminates the application.

question: Assume the target JVM (process 4242) runs Java 17. What is the expected result of this command?
code: jcmd 4242 Thread.dump_to_file -format=json /tmp/threads.json
options: jcmd reports an unknown diagnostic command, because Thread.dump_to_file was added in a later release (Java 21)
A JSON thread dump is written to the file
A heap dump is written to the file
explanation: Thread.dump_to_file, which can produce JSON dumps that include virtual threads, was introduced in Java 21. On Java 17 use Thread.print or jstack. Check the target JVM's version before copying commands from newer documentation.

question: What does the -l option of jstack add?
options: It forces a full garbage collection before printing
It limits the output to ten threads
It adds information about locked ownable synchronizers, such as java.util.concurrent locks, to the thread dump
It writes the dump in HPROF format
explanation: The long listing includes which threads own ReentrantLock-style synchronizers. Without it, only monitor information for synchronized blocks is complete, so j.u.c. lock holders are harder to find.

question: Which method completes the code so it reports whether any threads are deadlocked on monitors or ownable synchronizers?
explanation: ThreadMXBean.findDeadlockedThreads() returns the ids of deadlocked threads or null when there are none, so this program prints none. findMonitorDeadlockedThreads covers monitors only. The other names do not exist.

question: What is printed?
explanation: The default thread factory names threads pool-N-thread-M. Such generic names make thread dumps hard to read, which is why custom names are recommended.

question: What is printed?
explanation: The custom ThreadFactory names the first thread orders-1, because getAndIncrement returns 1 before incrementing. Meaningful thread names let you identify pools quickly in a thread dump.

question: A thread dump lists these thread states. Assume / means integer division. What is printed?
explanation: Three threads are BLOCKED, so the expression is 300 / 7. With integer division that is 42, not the rounded 43.

question: A thread dump shows a thread in state RUNNABLE inside a native socket read method. What can be concluded?
options: It may simply be waiting for network data and not consuming CPU, because the JVM reports threads in native I/O as RUNNABLE
It must be using 100% of a CPU core
It is blocked on a monitor
explanation: RUNNABLE means the thread is runnable from the JVM's point of view, which includes blocking native I/O calls. Correlate with per-thread CPU time (for example from top -H) before assuming it is a CPU hotspot.

question: A dump shows 20 threads named pool-2-thread-N in state WAITING (parking) inside LinkedBlockingQueue.take. What does this most likely mean?
options: The pool has too many tasks queued
They are idle workers waiting for tasks, which is normal
explanation: Worker threads of a ThreadPoolExecutor block on the work queue when there is nothing to do. Idle workers are not a problem. Look instead at threads stuck inside request-handling code.

question: All 50 request threads in several thread dumps are WAITING inside a connection pool's method that borrows a database connection. What is the most likely situation?
options: The connection pool is exhausted, so threads wait for a free connection; look for connection leaks or slow queries holding connections
explanation: Many threads parked at the same borrow call mean demand exceeds available connections. The fix is to find connections that are not returned or are held too long, rather than just enlarging heap or thread counts.

question: Which sequence finds the Java code behind a CPU-hungry native thread of a JVM on Linux?
options: Run jmap -histo, then restart the JVM
Take a heap dump, then search it for the thread id in decimal
Run top -H -p <pid>, convert the busy thread id to hex, then search for nid=0x<hex> in a jstack dump of that process
Run jstat -gc, then search the GC log for the thread id in decimal
explanation: top -H shows per-thread CPU. HotSpot prints the native thread id as hexadecimal nid in thread dumps, so converting the id lets you locate the exact Java thread and its stack.

question: One thread uses 100% CPU. In three dumps taken ten seconds apart it is RUNNABLE inside java.util.regex.Pattern internals, called from the same validation method. What is the most likely cause?
options: Catastrophic backtracking from a poorly written regular expression on certain input
explanation: A thread that is RUNNABLE in the same regex code across dumps while burning CPU points to a long-running match, typically exponential backtracking. The repeated identical stack shows it is not making progress elsewhere.

question: Thirty threads are BLOCKED waiting to lock the same monitor address. The only owner thread is inside a socket read while holding it. What is the best fix?
options: Do the slow I/O outside the synchronized block so the lock is held only briefly
explanation: The contention comes from holding a lock during slow I/O. Shrinking the critical section removes the queue of blocked threads, whereas more threads or heap only add more waiters.

question: An application stops responding to requests, but CPU is near zero and heap usage looks normal. Which artifact most directly shows why?
options: Several thread dumps taken seconds apart
explanation: A hang with low CPU usually means threads are waiting on locks, I/O or pools. Thread dumps show what each thread waits for and whether it changes over time. Heap and allocation data answer memory questions instead.

question: Which artifact lets you find the chain of references that keeps a large set of objects alive?
options: A heap dump analyzed with a path-to-GC-roots view
explanation: Only a heap dump contains the object graph. Analysis tools can show the shortest path from a GC root to the suspect objects, which tells you which reference to remove or clear.

question: Why should heap dumps be handled as sensitive files?
options: They can contain in-memory secrets and personal data such as passwords, tokens and request payloads
explanation: A heap dump copies the process's object data, so credentials and customer data present in memory can be read from it. Restrict access, store it securely and delete it after analysis.

question: A pod is restarted after an OutOfMemoryError, and the dump written to /tmp disappears with the container. What is the right fix?
options: Write the dump to standard output
Point -XX:HeapDumpPath to a persistent mounted volume with enough free space
explanation: Container file systems are usually ephemeral. A mounted volume sized for at least the used heap keeps the dump available after the restart.

question: Before taking a heap dump of a JVM with 6 GB of used heap, what should you plan for?
options: A file roughly the size of the used heap, enough free disk space, and a pause while the dump is written
No pause, because dumping is fully concurrent
A file of a few kilobytes
A dump that contains only thread stacks
explanation: HotSpot writes the dump at a safepoint, so application threads pause, and the file is about as large as the heap contents. Schedule it carefully and check disk space first.

question: Running jcmd 4242 Thread.print as a normal user fails to connect to a JVM owned by the user appsvc. What is the usual fix?
options: Run the command as the same operating system user as the target JVM, for example with sudo -u appsvc
explanation: The attach mechanism requires the same effective user as the target process (or suitable privileges). Running jcmd as that user solves it without restarting the application. Deleting /tmp files can even break attachment.

question: Which Eclipse MAT feature automatically proposes objects that hold an unusually large part of the heap?
explanation: The Leak Suspects report analyzes the dominator tree and highlights objects or groups that retain a suspiciously large share of memory, giving a fast starting point for investigation.

question: After several redeploys of a web application, a heap dump shows many instances of the same application ClassLoader and the JVM throws OutOfMemoryError: Metaspace. What is the likely cause?
options: The young generation is too small
The application has too many threads
Old classloaders are still strongly reachable, for example through ThreadLocals, static references or running threads, so their classes cannot be unloaded
explanation: Classes are unloaded only when their ClassLoader becomes unreachable. A lingering reference from a container thread or shared library keeps the old loader and all its classes in metaspace.

question: In an orchestrated environment you want the JVM to write a heap dump on OutOfMemoryError and then exit so that the orchestrator restarts it. Which flags do that (Java 17)?
explanation: HeapDumpOnOutOfMemoryError writes the dump and ExitOnOutOfMemoryError terminates the JVM afterwards, avoiding a half-working process. The other flags do not exist in HotSpot.

question: Which practice best summarizes reliable dump-based diagnosis?
options: Take one dump at startup and compare it with expected values
Take a heap dump after every request
Capture dumps while the problem is occurring, take several thread dumps over time, and correlate them with GC logs or metrics
explanation: Dumps are snapshots, so timing matters. Capturing during the incident, repeating thread dumps and combining them with other telemetry gives evidence rather than guesses.

question: What is printed? (Assume normal scheduling.)
explanation: A thread waiting for a ReentrantLock is parked through LockSupport, so its state is WAITING, not BLOCKED. Only waiting to enter a synchronized monitor gives BLOCKED. In a thread dump you identify the owner through the ownable synchronizer information.

question: What is printed?
explanation: Thread.getAllStackTraces() returns a map of all live threads to their stack traces, and the main thread is alive while running this code. It is the in-process equivalent of a thread dump.

question: What does latency measure?
options: The number of requests completed per second
The time one operation or request takes from start to completion
The percentage of CPU in use
The amount of heap occupied by live objects
explanation: Latency is the elapsed time of a single operation, usually reported as percentiles. Requests completed per second is throughput, and the other options describe resource usage.

question: What does throughput measure?
options: The time of the slowest request
The size of the Java heap
The amount of work completed per unit of time, such as requests per second
The number of threads in a pool
explanation: Throughput is the rate of completed work. A system can have high throughput and still have poor latency for individual requests, so the two must be measured separately.

question: By Little's Law (L = arrival rate x average time in system), a service handles 50 requests per second and each request takes 200 ms on average. How many requests are in the system on average?
explanation: L = 50 x 0.2 s = 10 requests in flight on average. The trap is forgetting to convert 200 ms to 0.2 seconds.

question: What does a p99 latency of 800 ms mean?
options: 99% of requests completed in 800 ms or less, and 1% took longer
Every request took at most 800 ms
explanation: A percentile is a threshold under which the stated share of observations fall. p99 describes the slowest 1% boundary, which is why it is used to describe tail latency.

question: Why can an average latency be misleading when analyzing user experience?
options: Averages cannot be computed for time values
The average is always equal to the median
A few very slow requests can be hidden by many fast ones, so the average hides tail behavior
The average only includes failed requests
explanation: Latency distributions are usually skewed. A good average can coexist with a bad p99 or p99.9, so percentiles or histograms should be reported.

question: Convention: arrays are 1-based and / is integer division. The array is already sorted. What is printed (nearest-rank percentile)?
explanation: rank = (900 + 99) / 100 = 999 / 100 = 9 with integer division. The ninth element of the sorted array is 16. The single outlier of 200 affects only the maximum.

question: What is the output?
explanation: The sum is 9 x 10 + 910 = 1000, and 1000 / 10 = 100 is the average. The maximum is 910. The average of 100 ms hides the fact that one request was nine times slower than that.

question: What is coordinated omission in load testing?
options: A load generator that waits for a slow response before sending the next request, so the delay it causes is missing from the recorded latencies
Running two load generators on one machine
Omitting warm-up from the report on purpose
explanation: When the tool is blocked by one slow response it stops generating the requests that should have been sent meanwhile, so the queueing delay those requests would have seen is never measured and tail latency looks better than reality.

question: What is the allocation rate of a Java application?
options: The number of classes loaded per minute
The amount of memory (or number of objects) the application allocates per unit of time
The percentage of the heap that is free
The number of garbage collections per hour
explanation: Allocation rate is usually quoted in MB/s. A high rate makes the young generation fill faster and therefore triggers more frequent young collections.

question: What is a TLAB (thread-local allocation buffer) in HotSpot?
options: A per-thread chunk of the young generation in which the thread allocates objects by bumping a pointer, without locking
A separate heap for large arrays
explanation: Each thread allocates from its own buffer, which makes ordinary object allocation very cheap and avoids contention on a shared allocation pointer.

question: Why are short-lived objects relatively cheap for a generational garbage collector?
options: They are never allocated on the heap
They are collected by the JIT compiler
A young collection copies only the live objects, so dead objects cost almost nothing to reclaim
explanation: Young-generation cost is proportional to the survivors, not to the garbage. Objects that die before the collection add no copying work, which is the generational hypothesis at work.

question: The program prints 4999950000. Which change removes most of the per-iteration allocation without changing the output?
options: Declare the loop variable i as Integer
Declare sum as the primitive type long
Replace the for loop with a while loop
explanation: sum += i unboxes the Long, adds, and boxes a new Long for values outside the small cache range, so each iteration allocates. A primitive long accumulator needs no allocation. Making i an Integer would add boxing, and final would not even compile with +=.

question: What is the output?
explanation: Integer.valueOf caches values from -128 to 127, so autoboxing 127 returns the same object, while 128 creates two separate objects. Values outside the cache allocate, and == compares references.

question: Why is building a large string with += inside a loop a performance problem?
options: Each concatenation creates a new String and copies the existing characters, causing quadratic copying and garbage; StringBuilder appends into one buffer
Strings cannot be concatenated more than 1000 times
It forces a full garbage collection on each iteration
explanation: Strings are immutable, so every += allocates a new String and copies the old content. A StringBuilder grows one internal array and avoids repeated copying.

question: Which argument completes the code so that the list never needs to resize its internal array while the loop adds elements?
explanation: The constructor argument is the initial capacity. With n the array is large enough from the start. 0 and 1 work but cause repeated growth and copying, and -1 throws IllegalArgumentException.

question: What is escape analysis in the HotSpot JIT compiler?
options: A check that finds methods that are never called
A tool that detects memory leaks in the heap
An analysis of whether an object can be seen outside the method or thread that creates it; if not, the JIT may avoid the heap allocation or remove locking
A security feature that blocks reflection
explanation: If an object does not escape, the compiled code can replace it with its fields (scalar replacement) and skip allocation. This is why tiny temporary objects are sometimes free in hot code.

question: Which object is the most likely candidate for scalar replacement by the JIT?
options: A Point created inside a hot method, used only for local arithmetic, and never stored, returned, or passed elsewhere
A Point added to a static list
A Point returned from the method
A Point passed to another thread
explanation: Scalar replacement requires that the object does not escape. Storing, returning, or publishing it makes it escape, so it must live on the heap.

question: Assume Java 17. Which command writes the GC log to gc.log?
explanation: Since Java 9 GC logging uses unified logging (-Xlog). PrintGCDetails and -Xloggc were removed or deprecated, and in Java 17 the first command fails to start because of an unrecognized option. The other commands are not valid options.

question: Which collector is designed mainly to maximize application throughput and accepts longer stop-the-world pauses?
explanation: Parallel GC uses multiple threads for stop-the-world collections and favors total throughput. ZGC and Shenandoah target short pauses, and Epsilon does not reclaim memory at all.

question: What does -XX:MaxGCPauseMillis=100 mean for the G1 collector?
options: It is a soft goal that G1 tries to meet by adjusting its work, not a hard guarantee
It guarantees that no pause will ever exceed 100 ms
It limits the heap to 100 MB
It stops the JVM after 100 pauses
explanation: G1 sizes the young generation and chooses regions to fit the goal when it can, but a pause may still be longer, for example during a full GC or with a heavy live set.

question: Assume Java 17. Which flag selects the ZGC collector?
explanation: ZGC has been a production feature since Java 15, so -XX:+UseZGC is enough in Java 17. The other flags select different collectors.

question: Convention: / is integer division. What is printed as the GC throughput percentage?
code:
app_seconds = 95
gc_seconds = 5
print(app_seconds * 100 / (app_seconds + gc_seconds))
explanation: Throughput here is the share of time spent running application code: 95 x 100 / 100 = 95. The remaining 5 percent is GC overhead.

question: A service groups many small database writes into one batch. What is the typical trade-off?
options: Both throughput and latency of each item always improve
Throughput usually improves, but each item may wait for the batch to fill, which increases its latency
explanation: Batching amortizes fixed costs such as round trips, raising throughput, but items wait before being sent. Choose batch size and maximum wait time according to the latency requirement.

question: One user request calls 100 backend services in parallel, and each service has a p99 of 200 ms. Roughly what share of user requests will see at least one backend call slower than its p99?
explanation: The chance that all 100 calls are fast is 0.99 raised to the power 100, about 37%, so about 63% see at least one slow call. This is tail latency amplification in fan-out systems.

question: According to Amdahl's Law, what is the maximum speedup for a task where 20% of the work is strictly serial, however many cores are added?
explanation: The speedup is limited by 1 / serial fraction = 1 / 0.2 = 5. The serial part always takes the same time, so adding cores cannot help beyond that.

question: For a thread pool that runs purely CPU-bound tasks, which size is a sensible starting point?
options: Ten times the number of cores
About the number of available CPU cores
The number of requests per second
explanation: CPU-bound work cannot run faster than the available cores, and extra threads only add context switching. Pools for blocking I/O can be larger, depending on the wait ratio.

question: Why does latency often grow sharply when a server's utilization approaches 100%?
options: Requests start to queue, and queueing delay grows non-linearly as the arrival rate approaches the service capacity
explanation: At low utilization requests are served immediately; near saturation any burst creates a queue whose waiting time dominates the response time. Keeping headroom protects tail latency.

question: Which clock is recommended for measuring elapsed time inside one JVM?
options: System.nanoTime(), because it is monotonic and not affected by wall-clock adjustments
new Date().getTime(), because it is the most precise
Instant.now(), because it ignores clock changes
explanation: nanoTime is intended for elapsed-time measurement and does not jump when the system clock is corrected. The other three read the wall clock, which can move backwards or forwards.

question: Each statement new Obj() creates one object. What is printed?
code:
count = 0
for i in 1..100:
    o = new Obj()
    count = count + 1
    for j in 1..10:
        p = new Obj()
        count = count + 1
print(count)
explanation: The outer loop allocates 100 objects and the inner loop allocates 100 x 10 = 1000 objects, which gives 1100 in total. Counting allocations in nested loops is how allocation rate is estimated by hand.

question: Which approach sums the numbers 1 to n for a large n without allocating a boxed Integer per element?
options: List<Integer> list filled with 1..n and then list.stream().reduce(0, Integer::sum)
explanation: IntStream works on primitive ints throughout. The other approaches create Integer objects (iterate, boxed, and the list), which adds allocation and GC work.

question: Why is calling String.format on a hot path often slower than simple concatenation or a StringBuilder?
options: String.format is not allowed in loops
It always throws on the second call
It converts every argument to a long
It parses the format string on each call and creates a Formatter and several temporary objects
explanation: String.format has to parse the format specification every time and allocates a Formatter, buffers and boxed arguments. For simple joins in hot code a StringBuilder is cheaper, though readability may still justify format elsewhere.

question: When is object pooling a poor idea in modern Java?
options: For small, cheap, short-lived objects, because allocation and young collection are very cheap and pools add contention and long-lived references
explanation: Pooling pays off for objects that are costly to create or are limited resources, such as connections and threads. For tiny temporary objects it usually slows the program down and can promote objects to the old generation.

question: The program prints true. What is the performance problem if isValid runs for every request, and what is the fix?
options: matches() is quadratic, so use find() instead
The regex is compiled on every call; keep one compiled Pattern in a static final field and reuse it
Pattern is not thread-safe, so every thread needs its own copy through a ThreadLocal
Strings must be interned before they are matched
explanation: Pattern.compile is expensive and its result is immutable and thread-safe, so it should be created once and shared. Only the lightweight Matcher is created per call.

question: Assume Java 17. What is printed?
explanation: A default StringBuilder starts with capacity 16. Appending 17 characters needs more room, and the buffer grows to old capacity x 2 + 2 = 34. Growth like this is why presizing a builder avoids copying.

question: Why do many production setups use the same value for -Xms and -Xmx?
options: It avoids pauses and work caused by resizing the heap while the application runs
explanation: A fixed heap size removes heap growth and shrink decisions at runtime and makes memory use more predictable. In containers you must still make sure the size fits the memory limit.

question: What does -XX:+AlwaysPreTouch do?
options: Touches every page of the heap at JVM startup so the operating system commits the memory early instead of during runtime allocation
Prevents any object from being garbage collected
explanation: Pre-touching moves page-fault cost to startup, which makes later allocation latency more predictable. The price is a slower start and immediate memory use.

question: A service creates many medium-lived objects that survive one young collection and are then promoted, filling the old generation too quickly. Which tuning step is most likely to help?
options: Give the young generation more room so objects have time to die before promotion
Decrease the number of CPU cores
explanation: Premature promotion happens when survivors are tenured before they die. A larger young generation (or survivor space) gives short-to-medium-lived objects more time to become garbage in the cheap young collection.

question: In G1, what is a humongous object?
options: An object with more than 100 fields
An object that has been referenced by more than one thread
An object whose size is at least half of a region, so it is allocated directly in contiguous old-generation regions
explanation: Humongous allocations bypass the young generation and need contiguous regions, which can cause fragmentation and extra GC activity. Large arrays are typical examples.

question: Which JMH option reports allocated bytes per operation?
explanation: The gc profiler of JMH reports allocation rate and normalized allocation per operation (gc.alloc.rate.norm), which is the key figure for judging whether a change reduced allocation.

question: What is a key property of ZGC regarding pause times?
options: Pause times do not grow in proportion to the heap size or the live set, because most work is done concurrently
Pause times grow linearly with the heap size
It always pauses for exactly one second
It never uses more than one thread
explanation: ZGC performs marking, relocation and reference processing concurrently, so stop-the-world pauses stay short even for very large heaps. It trades some throughput and CPU for that.

question: The array holds two values near two billion. Which type completes the code so it prints 4000000000 without boxing?
explanation: The sum exceeds Integer.MAX_VALUE, so int overflows and prints -294967296. A primitive long holds the result without allocation. Integer would overflow and box, and Object does not support +=.

question: Assume Java 17. What is true about the program?
options: It prints 1000000, because substring returns the same String
It prints 3, and small shares the big array so big stays reachable
It prints 3, and small holds its own copy, so big can be collected once nothing else references it
It prints 3, but only after intern() is called
explanation: Since Java 7u6 substring copies the characters, so the small string does not retain the large backing array. In very old releases, sharing could cause memory retention.

question: What is printed?
explanation: Because a is a final variable initialized with a constant, a + "b" is a compile-time constant and is folded into the interned literal. b is not final, so b + "b" is built at runtime as a new String. Constant folding avoids runtime allocation.

question: Which statement about lambdas and allocation in HotSpot is correct?
options: A lambda that captures no variables is typically a single cached instance, while a capturing lambda allocates a new object each time it is evaluated
Every lambda evaluation always allocates exactly one object
Lambdas can never be inlined by the JIT
Lambdas always run on a separate thread
explanation: Non-capturing lambdas have no per-evaluation state, so the runtime can reuse one instance. A lambda that captures values needs an object to store them, which may be removed by escape analysis if it does not escape.

question: What is a hidden allocation cost of calling a method declared as log(String fmt, Object... args) with arguments?
options: No cost, since varargs are free
Each call creates a new Object[] to hold the arguments, and primitive arguments are also boxed
The JVM creates one new thread per call
The arguments are written to disk
explanation: Varargs are implemented as an array created at the call site. In hot paths use fixed-arity overloads or guard the call, and avoid boxing primitives where possible.

question: Which logging statement avoids building an expensive message when the debug level is disabled?
explanation: Parameterized messages are formatted only when the level is enabled. The other forms concatenate or format the string before the call, so the work happens even when debug output is dropped.

question: Convention: / is integer division. What is printed as requests per second?
code:
requests = 6000
seconds = 30
print(requests / seconds)
explanation: Throughput is work divided by time: 6000 / 30 = 200 requests per second. Dividing in the wrong order or multiplying are common slips.

question: Convention: / is integer division. Using Little's Law, what is printed as the average number of requests in flight?
code:
arrival_per_second = 200
latency_ms = 50
print(arrival_per_second * latency_ms / 1000)
explanation: 200 x 50 = 10000, divided by 1000 gives 10 requests in flight. The division converts milliseconds to seconds. This value helps size thread and connection pools.

question: Convention: / is integer division. Four GC pauses of 10, 20, 30 and 40 ms occurred within a 1000 ms window. What is printed?
code:
pauses = [10, 20, 30, 40]
total = 0
for p in pauses:
    total = total + p
print(total * 100 / 1000)
explanation: The pauses add up to 100 ms, and 100 x 100 / 1000 = 10, so 10 percent of the window was spent paused. Total pause time matters for throughput, while the longest single pause matters for latency.

question: What is a benefit of recording latencies in an HdrHistogram instead of keeping only a running average?
options: It records values over a wide range with fixed memory and bounded error, so percentiles such as p99.9 can be reported
It removes the need for a load test
explanation: HdrHistogram stores counts in value buckets with a chosen precision, so percentiles can be read at any time without keeping every sample. An average alone cannot reveal the tail.

question: Why do the first requests after a JVM starts often have much higher latency than later ones?
options: The operating system forbids fast responses at the start
The heap is empty and cannot allocate
Logging is always slower at the start
Code runs in the interpreter and classes are loaded and JIT-compiled lazily, so warm-up work adds delay
explanation: Class loading, interpretation and JIT compilation are on-demand. Steady-state performance appears only after hot methods are compiled, so measure after warm-up unless startup latency is the goal.

question: What does a long time-to-safepoint (TTSP) mean for application latency?
options: The JVM has to wait for threads to reach a safepoint before a pause can begin, so all threads can be delayed longer than the pause work itself
explanation: Stop-the-world operations begin only when every thread has stopped at a safepoint. One thread running a long loop without polls delays everyone. Unified logging with -Xlog:safepoint reports these times.

question: Adding a large in-memory cache cut request latency. Which side effect should you check next?
options: The retained heap grows, which can lengthen GC work or cause promotion and pressure on the old generation
explanation: Cached objects stay reachable, so they increase the live set that collectors must manage. Latency gains from caching should be verified together with GC behavior and a bounded cache size.

question: Which choice matches the workload? A nightly batch job that processes billions of records versus an interactive API.
options: Optimize both for p50 latency only
Optimize the batch job for tail latency and the API for total throughput only
Favor throughput for the batch job, and favor low tail latency for the interactive API
Use the same tuning for both because goals never differ
explanation: A batch job is judged by total completion time, so throughput matters and longer pauses are acceptable. An interactive service is judged by the response time users see, so tail latency matters most.

question: Which statement is a common misconception?
options: Percentiles describe the latency distribution better than the average
Throughput and latency can move in opposite directions
Adding more threads always increases throughput
explanation: Throughput is limited by the scarcest resource, such as CPU, locks or a database. Beyond that point more threads add contention and context switching and can lower throughput while raising latency.

question: Which rule best summarizes tuning for latency, throughput and allocation?
options: Measure percentiles and allocation under a realistic load, find the real hot spots, change one thing at a time, and re-measure
Reduce allocation everywhere before any measurement
Report only the average of one run
explanation: Optimization should be driven by evidence from realistic load: percentiles for latency, rate for throughput and allocation per operation. Each change must be verified, otherwise effort goes into code that does not matter.

question: Assume Java 17. Which flag disables escape analysis, which helps check whether a lower allocation rate came from scalar replacement?
explanation: -XX:-DoEscapeAnalysis turns the analysis off, so objects that were eliminated are allocated again. Comparing allocation numbers with and without it shows how much the optimization contributes.

question: A G1 log line says "Pause Young (Normal) (G1 Evacuation Pause)". What does it describe?
options: A full collection triggered by System.gc()
A stop-the-world young collection, usually started because eden filled, that copies live objects to survivor or old regions
explanation: Normal young pauses are the regular result of allocation filling eden. A high allocation rate makes them more frequent, and a large survivor set makes each one longer.

question: What is the output?
explanation: A new int array is zero-filled by the JVM, which is part of the cost of allocating large arrays. Only index 1 is assigned, so the output is [0, 5, 0]. Primitive arrays never contain null.

question: Which statement about ByteBuffer.allocateDirect is correct?
options: Direct buffers cost more to allocate and live outside the Java heap, so hot paths should reuse them instead of allocating one per operation
Direct buffers are cheaper to allocate than heap buffers
Direct buffers are collected immediately after allocation
explanation: Direct buffer memory is native, comes with extra allocation and cleanup cost, and is limited by -XX:MaxDirectMemorySize rather than -Xmx. Reusing buffers avoids both the cost and native memory growth.

question: What is JMH?
options: A garbage collector for very large heaps
A harness for writing, running and analyzing Java micro-benchmarks, developed within the OpenJDK project
A tool that compiles Java to native executables
A JVM flag that profiles memory usage
explanation: JMH (Java Microbenchmark Harness) generates the benchmark code, handles forking, warm-up and measurement, and reports statistics. It is not a collector, a compiler or a JVM flag.

question: Which pair of Maven dependencies is needed to write and build JMH benchmarks?
explanation: jmh-core provides the annotations and runtime, and jmh-generator-annprocess is the annotation processor that generates the benchmark harness code at compile time.

question: What does the @Benchmark annotation do?
options: Runs a method once before the JVM starts
Excludes a method from JIT compilation
Marks a public method as a benchmark that JMH generates code to call repeatedly and measure
explanation: Only methods annotated with @Benchmark are measured. The annotation processor generates the loop, timing and fork code around them.

question: What does @State(Scope.Thread) mean?
options: One state instance is shared by all benchmark threads
Each benchmark thread gets its own instance of the state object
A new state object is created for every method call
The state is stored on disk between runs
explanation: Scope.Thread gives every benchmark thread a private instance, so threads do not share or contend on its fields.

question: Which scope is appropriate when all benchmark threads must exercise one shared object, such as a concurrent cache?
options: Scope.Group with a different group per thread
explanation: Scope.Benchmark creates a single instance shared by all threads running that benchmark, which is what you need to measure contention on a shared structure. Scope.Invocation does not exist.

question: What does Mode.AverageTime report?
options: The number of operations per second
The time of the first call only
explanation: AverageTime reports time per operation (for example ns/op), whereas Throughput reports operations per time unit. They are inverses of each other, not the same number.

question: Assume JMH on Java 17. Which benchmark method is most likely to be optimized away by dead code elimination?
explanation: The result of Math.sqrt(x) in the discarded benchmark is never used, so the JIT may remove the call. JMH consumes returned values and values passed to a Blackhole, which keeps that work alive.

question: Why can reading a compile-time constant in a benchmark give misleadingly fast results?
options: Constants cannot be read by the JIT
The JIT can fold computations on constants at compile time, so little or nothing is measured at run time
explanation: If the inputs are known constants, the compiler can precompute the result. Reading inputs from non-final @State fields keeps the computation real.

question: What is the purpose of warm-up iterations in JMH?
options: They check the syntax of the benchmark
They let class loading, the JIT compiler and caches reach a steady state, and their results are discarded
They run the benchmark on a second machine
They increase the number of forks
explanation: Early iterations include interpretation and compilation, which is not representative of steady-state performance. Warm-up results are not included in the final score.

question: Which annotation configures the number and duration of the measured iterations?
explanation: @Measurement sets iterations and time per iteration for the recorded runs. @Warmup does the same for the discarded warm-up phase, @Fork sets the number of JVMs and @Threads sets the number of benchmark threads.

question: Why does JMH run each benchmark in separate forked JVMs?
options: To isolate the benchmark from profile and JIT state left by earlier benchmarks, and to expose run-to-run variance
To make benchmarks run in parallel with each other
explanation: JIT decisions depend on the type and branch profiles collected so far, so a fresh JVM per fork avoids pollution from other benchmarks. Several forks also show how much results vary between JVM runs.

question: Which annotation sets the unit, such as nanoseconds or microseconds, in which results are reported?
explanation: @OutputTimeUnit takes a java.util.concurrent.TimeUnit and makes the score read, for example, ns/op or ops/ms.

question: When does a method annotated with @Setup(Level.Trial) run?
options: Once per benchmark trial (per fork), before its iterations start
explanation: Trial level setup runs once for each fork before warm-up and measurement. Iteration and Invocation levels run more often.

question: What does @Param do in a JMH state class?
options: It passes a parameter to the main method
It declares a method parameter that must be null
It lists values for a field, and JMH runs the benchmark once for each value
explanation: @Param lets one benchmark be measured for several inputs, such as different collection sizes, without copying code. The values can also be overridden on the command line with -p.

question: Why is putting a manual loop of one million iterations inside a @Benchmark method discouraged?
